title: QVIC-Global™ — Cryptographic Migration Governance and Prioritization Framework: Commercial Intellectual Property Asset, Licensing Technology, and Enterprise Governance Platform
abstract: QVIC-Global™ — Cryptographic Migration Governance and Prioritization Framework GLOBAL ECOSYSTEM RELEASE v1.1.2 TECHNICAL DOCUMENTATION | MIGRATION ASSESSMENT MODEL | ADVISORY PLANNING DEMONSTRATOR | SOFTWARE VERIFICATION | RELEASE INTEGRITY AUTHORSHIP AND RELEASE IDENTIFICATION Author: Bidyut Mazumdar Research Profile: Independent Researcher–Scholar ORCID: https://orcid.org/0009-0007-5615-3558 Project Designation: QVIC-Global™ Release: Global Ecosystem Release v1.1.2 Release Date: 15 October 2026 Resource Type: Software Technical Domains: Post-Quantum Cryptography, Cryptographic Migration Planning, Cybersecurity Governance, Digital Infrastructure Resilience, and Technology Risk Assessment Implementation Classification: Research-Stage Framework and Python-Based Advisory Planning Demonstrator Operational Classification: Advisory Only Production Deployment: Not Established Independent Security Certification: Not Established Independent Empirical Validation: Not Established Persistent Identifier: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18378901 1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY QVIC-Global™ is a research-stage framework for structuring cryptographic migration assessments, generating preliminary prioritization estimates, and supporting governance-oriented planning for organizations preparing for the transition toward post-quantum cryptography (PQC). Cryptographic migration is not limited to replacing one algorithm with another. It can involve interconnected applications, authentication services, cryptographic libraries, digital certificates, communication protocols, key-management systems, legacy components, third-party dependencies, and information assets requiring long-term confidentiality. Changes to cryptographic components may affect interoperability, system dependencies, operational availability, implementation assurance, configuration integrity, and established security assumptions. Consequently, migration planning benefits from an explicit distinction between observed technical facts, manually supplied assessment values, model-generated estimates, and formally authorized engineering decisions. QVIC-Global™ addresses a defined subset of this problem through a Migration Assessment Template (MAT), a weighted linear prioritization model, structured JSON assessment records, JSON Schema-related validation assets, a Python-based planning demonstrator, automated tests, technical documentation, and release-integrity evidence. The v1.1.2 implementation provides a limited advisory workflow. It processes manually supplied assessment factors and calculates preliminary numerical priority estimates. Where required assessment information is missing or invalid, the implementation may prevent a complete score from being generated. The central design objective is to make selected migration-prioritization assumptions explicit, computationally inspectable, and suitable for structured human review. The current release must not be interpreted as an autonomous cryptographic discovery platform, a production migration controller, a cryptographic algorithm implementation, or an independently validated security-assurance system. QVIC-Global™ is therefore presented as a research-stage planning framework and software demonstrator. Its outputs are preliminary decision-support information, not verified security findings, mandatory migration instructions, or substitutes for qualified cryptographic engineering. 2. RESEARCH PROBLEM AND DESIGN RATIONALE 2.1. The Cryptographic Migration Challenge The transition toward post-quantum cryptography introduces technical and organizational planning requirements for systems that depend on cryptographic mechanisms to protect information, authenticate identities, establish secure communications, and maintain digital trust. Migration programmes may need to consider: • Cryptographic inventory: Identifying the algorithms, protocols, certificates, libraries, keys, and cryptographic services used by relevant systems. • Dependency analysis: Understanding relationships between applications, infrastructure components, external services, and cryptographic implementations. • Exposure assessment: Examining relevant exposure conditions and the consequences of cryptographic compromise. • Data-lifetime considerations: Evaluating how long information may require confidentiality or integrity protection. • Migration sequencing: Considering dependencies, interoperability requirements, implementation constraints, and operational change windows. • Uncertainty management: Distinguishing verified facts from incomplete information, estimates, and assumptions. • Rollback planning: Assessing whether a proposed change can be reversed safely and what constraints may complicate recovery. • Governance and accountability: Recording the rationale for prioritization and ensuring that consequential decisions remain subject to authorized human review. These considerations are related but are not interchangeable. A scoring model cannot independently establish the vulnerability of a system, verify the security of an implementation, determine regulatory compliance, or prove that a migration sequence is technically safe. 2.2. Defined Research Scope QVIC-Global™ addresses the narrower problem of representing selected migration-assessment considerations in a structured format and combining supplied factor values through an explicit weighted calculation. Its purpose is to support preliminary planning discussions and make the calculation process inspectable. The framework does not claim to resolve cryptographic discovery, dependency mapping, migration engineering, algorithm selection, security assurance, or enterprise-wide risk management in their entirety. 2.3. Design Principles The framework is organized around the following principles: Explicit Assumptions: Assessment inputs and configured weights should be identifiable and reviewable. Structured Representation: Assessment records should follow a defined data structure. Computational Transparency: The calculation should be expressible as an inspectable mathematical model. Input Discipline: Missing, malformed, or out-of-range values should not silently be treated as valid assessments. Bounded Interpretation: Numerical outputs should not be presented as more authoritative than the underlying model and evidence justify. Human Accountability: Consequential operational decisions should remain with appropriately qualified and authorized decision-makers. Reproducibility: The release should provide sufficient implementation and verification information to support inspection of the checks actually performed. These are design objectives. Their implementation and effectiveness remain subject to the capabilities and evidence available in the specific release. 3. TECHNICAL SCOPE AND RELEASE ARCHITECTURE The v1.1.2 release contains five principal functional and documentary components. 3.1. Migration Assessment Template The Migration Assessment Template (MAT) provides a structured representation of selected attributes associated with cryptographic migration work items. Cryptographic migration is not limited to replacing one algorithm with another. It can involve interconnected applications, authentication services, cryptographic libraries, digital certificates, communication protocols, key-management systems, legacy components, third-party dependencies, and information assets requiring long-term confidentiality. Changes to cryptographic components may affect interoperability, system dependencies, operational availability, implementation assurance, configuration integrity, and established security assumptions. title: Learning with Communication in Multi-agent Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Communication enables cooperating agents to coordinate their behavior and to access information about the environment. In multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL), communication protocols can be learned rather than predefined, alongside agents' value functions and policies. However, learning effective communication remains challenging in environments that are stochastic, continuous, or multi-task. This thesis addresses these challenges with the aim of improving learning stability, learning efficiency, and task performance through learnable and adaptive communication. First, we survey the literature on MADRL with communication and propose a classification framework of nine dimensions that capture key aspects of communication design and learning. The framework provides a structured basis for analyzing, comparing, and developing communication methods. Second, we study the Communicating Critics and Decentralized Actors (CCDA) setting, in which critics exchange messages during training while actors act without communication at execution. Under stated assumptions on ideal and noisy communication, we show that the variance of policy gradients under communicating critics is equal to or greater than that obtained with a centralized critic that has access to the complete joint information. To mitigate this variance, we derive a message-dependent baseline, characterize its variance-minimizing form, and propose a complementary regularization technique. Experiments show reduced gradient variance and improved learning performance. Third, we propose Communication with Factorized Policy Gradients (CFPG) for continuous control. CFPG uses centralized but factorized value functions to distinguish the contribution of each communicating agent, and propagates gradients through both policies and message encoders so that communication and action selection are learned jointly. Experiments in continuous-control benchmarks show improved performance and faster learning relative to the evaluated baselines. Finally, we introduce Multi-task Communication Skills (MCS), a Transformer-based method that enables agents to learn and perform multiple tasks with a single shared communication protocol. The protocol accommodates varying numbers of agents as well as heterogeneous observation and action spaces by encoding task-specific observations into a shared message space, limiting unnecessary communication, and aggregating received messages. An additional learning objective encourages messages to carry information about the senders' actions. Together, these contributions provide theoretical insights and practical methods for learning communication in cooperative MADRL. Evaluations on simulated benchmarks demonstrate improvements in learning stability, efficiency, or task performance relative to the evaluated baselines, with the magnitude of improvement varying across tasks.

title: FROM PIXELS TO PROMPTS: A STRUCTURED NARRATIVE REVIEW OF SECURITY, PRIVACY, AND ADVERSARIAL ROBUSTNESS IN HEALTHCARE AI
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare, where evaluations usually ask whether a system is accurate on ordinary clinical data. This review asks instead what can happen when someone deliberately changes the data, instructions, or training to make a system fail, behave in hidden ways, or reveal confidential information, a field known as adversarial machine learning. We reviewed 113 publications (2018–2026) and grouped the reported threats into six categories: altering an input after training; corrupting the training examples; teaching a hidden rule triggered later; using the model to learn private information; placing malicious instructions in language or image-and-language models; and attacking models trained jointly across hospitals or devices. Laboratory studies showed that small deliberate changes to medical images could alter a diagnosis or a model's outline, corrupted training data could change what a model learned, and malicious prompts could produce unsafe medical responses. Effect sizes varied greatly across models, datasets, attacks, and test conditions. Several defenses helped in individual experiments, but no single defense was shown to work across all threats and settings; in one imaging study, attacks tailored to the tested defenses bypassed all five. The studies do not show how often these attacks occur in practice or harm patients; their value is to demonstrate possible failure modes under controlled conditions. Medical AI should therefore be evaluated both on ordinary clinical data and in clearly described, clinically plausible attack scenarios.

title: Federated learning with adaptive reliability aware aggregation for privacy preserving healthcare IoT systems
abstract: Abstract Healthcare Internet of Things (IoT) devices generate vast amounts of sensitive patient data, creating significant privacy risks and regulatory challenges when processed through centralized architectures. Federated Learning (FL) offers a promising solution by enabling decentralized model training without sharing raw data. However, real-world deployment faces critical challenges including device heterogeneity, intermittent connectivity, non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data, and unreliable node participation. This paper proposes a Reliability-Aware Adaptive Aggregation (RAAA) framework that dynamically evaluates client trustworthiness through three dimensions: update quality (local accuracy and gradient alignment), participation consistency (historical engagement patterns), and communication latency. These metrics are integrated into a composite reliability score using weighted aggregation, which adaptively prioritizes contributions from trustworthy nodes during global model updates. The framework was validated using PhysioNet electrocardiogram (ECG) datasets (MIT-BIH and PTB) with 20 simulated healthcare IoT clients under conditions of node dropout and data heterogeneity. Experimental results demonstrate that RAAA achieved 91.7% classification accuracy on arrhythmia detection, outperforming Federated Averaging (FedAvg) (85.2%), Federated Proximal (FedProx) (86.4%), and Q-FedAvg (87.1%) by 6.5%, 5.3%, and 4.6%, respectively. The proposed method converged 17% faster (43 versus 52 rounds) and maintained an 85.6% client participation rate. Cross-dataset validation on the PTB database confirmed consistent improvements across different physiological signals. The RAAA framework provides a robust, privacy-preserving FL solution for healthcare IoT environments with superior accuracy, faster convergence, and resilience to unreliable nodes. All evaluations are conducted in a simulated environment; while theoretical energy and complexity analyses suggest suitability for resource-constrained edge devices, real-hardware validation remains an important direction for future work.

title: CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests
abstract: Context: Organizations increasingly delegate code review to multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines billed per token. Low code quality raises human maintenance effort, but its effect on agent review cost has not been measured. Objective: We test whether baseline CodeHealth predicts the token cost of agentic review and fix beyond pull request (PR) footprint. Method: In a pre-registered observational study, we sampled 465 agent-authored PRs from 246 repositories in AIDev, jointly stratified by CodeHealth and footprint under repository caps. A frozen five-agent review-and-fix pipeline processed every PR with three different LLMs. Per LLM, we fitted a mixed model of log tokens on CodeHealth and log PR footprint, with a repository random intercept. Results: For all three LLMs the CodeHealth coefficient was negative, with 95% CI excluding zero; each CodeHealth point was associated with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost. CodeHealth was unrelated to PR footprint, so PR size does not explain the association. Two of three registered smells predicted fix cost; batch fixing left median CodeHealth unchanged. Exploratory analyses located the association in the review stage, where agents iterated more on unhealthy code without writing more comments. Adjusting for the size of the scored files absorbed the association, which we interpret as mediation by file size. Conclusions: A quality metric calibrated against human maintainability also predicts the inference cost of multi-agent review and fix. The effect is modest per point and not carried by PR size, so the refactoring case extends to agent-reviewed code when it changes structure and file size, not only the score. Data Availability: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22127920

title: Hear, Localize, and Reason: Spatially Aware Scene Understanding for Audio-Visual LLMs
abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) have made strong progress in multimodal understanding, yet most treat audio as monaural semantic content, limiting their ability to reason about where sounds originate and how they relate to the visual scene. Recent spatial audio-visual studies address parts of this problem, but often focus on specific abilities, such as spatial correspondence or direction and distance reasoning. In this work, we introduce HLR-AVSceneQA, a comprehensive benchmark with a hear-localize-reason hierarchy that evaluates whether models can recognize what is heard, localize sound sources in egocentric and allocentric views, and use these localized sources to reason about how they relate to the visual scene. We further introduce HLR-LLM, which augments a strong audio-visual foundation model with a binaural spatial audio branch alongside its monaural semantic audio pathway. We train HLR-LLM with a curriculum that incorporates final-stage chain-of-thought supervision for multi-step spatial reasoning. Experiments show that existing AV-LLMs remain limited in spatial grounding and relational reasoning, while HLR-LLM substantially improves spatial audio-visual scene understanding without compromising semantic audio-visual perception.

title: Sparse Attention for Video Generation Acceleration via Growing Sparsity and Reduced Search
abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) dominate video generation but suffer from high inference cost due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Sparse attention mitigates this by skipping unnecessary computation in the attention matrix, but existing methods apply a fixed sparsity ratio throughout denoising and struggle to accurately determine which computations to skip. To address these limitations, we analyze attention dynamics through attention entropy and mean attention distance, and find that attention becomes increasingly concentrated across denoising steps. We further observe that blocks selected early continue to capture a large fraction of the total attention weight at later steps. These findings suggest two acceleration opportunities: the sparsity ratio should grow as denoising progresses, and earlier search results can be reused to reduce the search space. Based on these findings, we propose Growing Sparsity and Reduced Search (GSRS), a training-free framework that retains more computation early and progressively reduces it later, while restricting subsequent searches to an early candidate set to reduce search overhead. GSRS adopts Top-p selection for adaptive sparsity control, supported by a precise evaluation scheme that computes exact attention weights within the FlashAttention computation at negligible overhead. Experiments on HunyuanVideo and Wan 2.1 validate that GSRS achieves 1.55$\times$--2.21$\times$ speedup while maintaining generation quality comparable to full attention.

title: Rare Event Simulation of Quantum Error-Correcting Circuits
abstract: We describe a practical approach for accessing the logical failure rates of quantum error-correcting (QEC) circuits under low physical (component) failure rate regimes. Standard Monte Carlo is often the de facto approach for studying the failure rates of quantum circuits. However, in the study of fault-tolerant error-correcting circuits, the ability to extend this approach to low physical failure rates is limited. In particular, the use of Monte Carlo to access circuits that are relatively large or have high correcting power becomes more difficult as we lower the input failure rates of the individual components (gates) in the circuit. For these reasons, many simulations studying the circuit model go no lower than end-to-end logical failure rates in the 10 − 6 regime.In this report, we outline an approach that borrows from earlier work by Bravyi and Vargo \cite{bv13} to the more complex circuit noise model. Earlier works studied both the capacity and phenomenological noise models \cite{bv13,Beverland2019,bonilla2021xzzx}, but the work is insufficient for generating similar simulations in the circuit-noise model. To the best of our knowledge, our team is the first to develop a full prescription of the rare event simulation by splitting technique for the circuit-based noise model. We have also generated promising results that are confirmed by standard Monte Carlo simulation under an accessible regime. This work shows that we can access noise in the circuit-model prescription of quantum error-correcting code to failure rates below 10 − 20 regime.

title: Constraining Tool Authority in AI Agents: A Risk-Tiered Framework for Mitigating Indirect Prompt Injection
abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents read untrusted content, such as emails, web pages, and documents, and act through tools. Instructions hidden in that content can steer the agent, and the agent's permissions can turn that influence into unauthorized actions. This paper proposes a risk-based authorization architecture that reduces the consequences of indirect prompt injection without assuming the model resists it. The architecture separates model-generated action proposals from execution authority and combines task-scoped capabilities, a deterministic authorization gateway, risk-tiered approval bound to the exact proposed action, constrained tool interfaces, and security audit records. We state a threat model, six security objectives, and a control flow; position the design against recent architectural defenses (CaMeL, design patterns for prompt-injection-resistant agents, Progent, AgentSpec, and ClawGuard); and specify a reproducible evaluation protocol using instrumented mock tools and synthetic data. No prototype, benchmark run, or empirical result is reported. The contribution is a design and an evaluation protocol, not a validated defense, and the design is not claimed to be novel in its individual principles.

title: Adaptive Self-Search and Collaborative Search in World-Level Self–Mutual Models: A Unified Framework for Autonomous and Cooperative Search
abstract: Search is a fundamental operation in intelligent systems because it enables the discovery of states, solutions, relationships, strategies, and possible futures. Conventional search mechanisms often follow a predetermined search policy, while collaborative search systems rely on interactions among multiple agents, models, or computational processes. Although these approaches can be effective, autonomous search and collaborative search have different computational costs, information requirements, and problem-solving capabilities. A system that always searches independently may fail to exploit useful external knowledge, whereas a system that always collaborates may incur unnecessary communication, coordination, and evaluation costs. This paper proposes the Adaptive Self–Mutual World Search (ASMW-Search) framework, a conceptual architecture that integrates self-models, mutual-models, and world models to support adaptive transitions between self-search and collaborative search. The framework is not designed as a large language model or as a language-model-based multi-agent system. Instead, it treats the world model as a structured representation of environmental states, transitions, constraints, relationships, uncertainties, and potential outcomes. The self-model maintains an internal representation of the system's own knowledge, capabilities, search history, limitations, and predictions. The mutual-model represents relationships between the self-model and other models, including differences in knowledge, complementary capabilities, dependencies, and potential contributions to a search task. The proposed architecture selects among autonomous search, collaborative search, and intermediate forms of interaction according to estimated uncertainty, expected information gain, predicted search progress, computational cost, and the value of coordination. It further incorporates search-result integration, model updating, switching control, and feedback-driven adaptation. A formal decision objective is introduced to balance solution quality, search efficiency, communication overhead, and robustness. The paper defines research questions, testable hypotheses, an experimental design, evaluation metrics, limitations, and potential applications. As a conceptual proposal, the framework does not claim demonstrated performance or established superiority. Its central contribution is a unified research formulation in which autonomous and collaborative search are treated as dynamically selectable operating modes of a world-level self–mutual modeling system.

title: World Self–Mutual Models: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Planning and Collaborative Planning
abstract: World models provide internal representations of environmental states, transition dynamics, and possible future outcomes, enabling agents to plan actions before executing them. However, planning systems may face a fundamental architectural trade-off: independent planning can reduce communication and coordination costs but may lack complementary information, whereas collaborative planning can improve information coverage and resolve conflicting predictions but introduces additional computational and communication overhead. This paper proposes the World Self–Mutual Planning Framework (WSMPF), a conceptual architecture that integrates world models with two complementary planning modes: self-planning and collaborative planning. Self-planning enables an individual model to construct, evaluate, and revise its own action sequences using its internal world model. Collaborative planning enables multiple interacting models to exchange selected state representations, predictions, constraints, and candidate plans to construct or refine a coordinated plan. A meta-planning controller adaptively selects between these modes according to uncertainty, predicted task difficulty, plan disagreement, expected coordination benefit, communication cost, and execution risk. The framework is model-agnostic and does not require large language models. Its central hypothesis is that planning architecture should be selected dynamically rather than fixed permanently to either independent or collaborative operation. The paper formalizes the planning problem, defines a switching mechanism, presents an implementable algorithm, and proposes an experimental protocol for evaluating task success, planning quality, computational cost, communication overhead, robustness, and switching stability. The framework is presented as a research proposal; its empirical effectiveness and novelty relative to the complete existing literature remain to be established.

title: World Self-and-Mutual Models: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Diagnosis and Mutual Diagnosis for World-State Understanding and Model Reliability
abstract: World models provide computational representations of environmental states, transitions, and potential outcomes. However, a world model may contain internal inconsistencies, inaccurate state estimates, incorrect transition predictions, or assumptions that no longer correspond to the environment. Diagnosing these problems is therefore essential for maintaining reliable world representations. Existing research has investigated model-based diagnosis, multi-agent fault diagnosis, self-correction, and collaborative reasoning, but these research directions do not, by themselves, establish a unified framework in which self-diagnosis and mutual diagnosis are adaptively selected as complementary operating modes within a world-model architecture. This paper proposes the World Self-and-Mutual Models (WSMM) framework, a conceptual architecture that combines world-model-based state representation with a higher-level self-and-mutual modeling principle. WSMM distinguishes two diagnostic modes. In self-diagnosis, an individual world model examines its own state estimates, transition predictions, internal constraints, and accumulated discrepancies. In mutual diagnosis, multiple world models examine one another's predictions, compare their representations, and investigate inconsistencies that cannot be adequately resolved through isolated analysis. A diagnostic controller dynamically selects between these modes according to uncertainty, prediction error, disagreement, diagnostic confidence, task risk, computational cost, and the expected value of additional evidence. The framework formalizes world-state estimation, diagnostic discrepancy, mode selection, cross-model evidence integration, and model updating. It also introduces a distinction between diagnosing the state of the external world and diagnosing the internal reliability of the model representing that world. This distinction is important because an apparent environmental anomaly may originate from a faulty model, incomplete observations, an incorrect transition assumption, or a genuine change in the environment. The proposed framework is independent of any particular model architecture and does not require large language models. It can be implemented using predictive state-space models, robotics models, simulation systems, scientific models, or heterogeneous computational representations. Finally, the paper develops research questions, testable hypotheses, evaluation metrics, baseline comparisons, and a reproducible experimental design. The proposed framework is conceptual and has not yet been empirically validated; its principal contribution is a formal research direction for adaptive switching between individual and cross-model diagnosis in world-model systems.

title: Doctrinal Problems of Applying Copyright to Literary Works Created by Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The article analyses five doctrinal problems in applying copyright to literary works created by artificial intelligence (AI). First, it shows that the classical theories (Locke’s labour theory, Hegel’s personality theory, the utilitarian theory and the fair remuneration theory) come into conflict when applied to AI activity. Second, it examines the concept of “author” under the legislation of Uzbekistan, Russia and the United States and under the Berne Convention, together with the question of AI subjecthood. Third, it addresses the originality requirement, fourth, moral rights, and fifth, the idea–expression dichotomy. The author concludes that all these problems share a single cause: classical doctrines rest on human consciousness, will and personality. Accordingly, AI should be treated as a tool rather than a subject. The article also proposes the “objective control criterion doctrine”, which ties the emergence of copyright to objective, verifiable criteria: purposeful direction of AI activity, creative selection among outputs, and determination of the work’s final content and form.

title: TRACE: Topology-Aware Reconnection via Prediction-Adaptive Connectivity Enforcement for Thin-Structure Segmentation
abstract: Thin, elongated structures are particularly sensitive to connectivity errors, as even a few local segmentation mistakes can disrupt otherwise continuous paths. Existing skeleton-based objectives typically supervise fixed centerline locations and do not account for alternative local routes that may restore connectivity. We propose TRACE, a topology-aware, prediction-adaptive objective that uses a target skeleton to define required local connections. For each connection, TRACE identifies the easiest valid reconnection under the current prediction and jointly supervises its bottleneck with the corresponding skeleton point. The supervision thus adapts to the evolving prediction rather than remaining fixed to the centerline. We further introduce a topology-aware skeleton carrier that preserves both foreground and class-specific topology, enabling reliable definition of these connections. Extensive experiments across six 2D and 3D benchmarks show that TRACE improves connectivity and topology while maintaining strong segmentation accuracy with low training overhead. Code will be released upon acceptance.

title: AVALON: Zero-Shot Indoor Navigation with Human-Seeded Topological Memory
abstract: Indoor service robots often enter unmapped buildings whose layouts and task constraints are already familiar to users. We address this human-familiar, robot-unseen setting with AVALON, a topological navigation framework organized around human-seeded layered spatial memory, node-verified topological execution, and task-triggered, evidence-gated human--robot memory co-updating. The robot has no prior on-site traversal or site-specific training. Deployment requires only a floor plan, place clues, and an initial topology-odometry alignment. Visual depth point-goal navigation leverages verified node arrivals to perform translational re-anchoring, without requiring a robot-constructed global SLAM map. Human--robot memory co-updating fuses complementary sources of information. Human operators specify task constraints that are unobservable via vision and report offline environmental modifications, whereas the robot provides physical-state evidence through active in-situ validation. Task relevance governs whether human-reported environmental changes undergo robot validation during the active mission. Field-collected perceptual evidence gates memory updates, maintaining an explicit separation between human-specified permissions and robot-observed traversability. Our experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that AVALON with X-NavDP completes a 12.81 m Intersection-to-Dining mission in 46.4 s (5/5) with no mapping, 40.9% less robot time than DimOS-Go2 (78.5 s, 4/5), while policy-only X-NavDP times out in all of the 5 runs. These demonstrate the superiority of the proposed topological navigation framework.

title: Graph neural networks for transmission grid topology control: Busbar information asymmetry and heterogeneous representations
abstract: Factors such as the proliferation of renewable energy and electrification contribute to grid congestion which is a pressing problem. Topology control is an appealing method for relieving congestion, but traditional approaches for topology discovery have proven too slow for practical applications. Recent research has focused on machine learning (ML) as an efficient alternative. Due to their ability to model the graph structure of power grids, graph neural networks (GNNs) are particularly well-suited for topology control applications. This study investigates different graph representations of the power grid for topology control with GNNs. We identify an information flow problem inherent to the popular homogeneous graph representation and propose a heterogeneous graph representation that resolves said problem. We apply GNNs with both graph representations and a fully connected neural network (FCNN) baseline to an imitation learning task. The models are evaluated by classification accuracy and the percentage of successful grid operation days. We find that heterogeneous GNNs perform the best, followed by FCNNs, and lastly, homogeneous GNNs. We also find that both GNN types generalize better to unseen network configurations than FCNNs.

title: Auxiliary modalities add no detectable discrimination or calibration over structured EHR for 30-day COPD readmission: evidence from a leakage-audited MIMIC-IV cohort
abstract: Background: Hospital readmission is a common and costly outcome in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Multimodal deep learning models combining structured electronic health record (EHR) data with physiological, imaging, and textual data have been proposed to improve its prediction, but whether such fusion outperforms EHR data alone, once temporal-leakage safeguards are applied, remains unclear. Methods: Using a stratified MIMIC-IV cohort of COPD patients enriched to about 50% readmission (natural prevalence 18.1%; n=1,279; 895/192/192 training/validation/test), we predicted 30-day, all-cause readmission from four frozen, pre-trained encoders (electrocardiogram, chest radiograph, clinical notes, structured EHR). We audited and corrected temporal leakage in the admission-linkage pipeline of each modality, then compared three fusion architectures (naive concatenation, scalar gated fusion, EHR-anchored residual fusion) against unimodal baselines and an EHR-alone reference, using bootstrap significance testing, a missingness stress test, and calibration analysis with and without post-hoc recalibration. Results: The audit corrected three previously undetected temporal-alignment issues, affecting 5-9% of patients for clinical notes, 29-43% for chest radiographs, and 53-58% for ECG. After correction, every modality except EHR showed near-chance discrimination alone (ROC-AUC 0.46-0.53), confirmed with a non-linear adapter probe. No fusion architecture significantly outperformed the EHR-alone baseline (ROC-AUC 0.63); removing auxiliary modalities improved rather than degraded fusion performance under stress testing. The raw Brier score was lower for all three fusion architectures than for EHR-alone (about 0.24 versus 0.32), but this reflected overconfidence of the EHR-alone probe (calibration slope 0.12); after logistic recalibration fitted on the validation set, Brier scores were indistinguishable (EHR-alone 0.239; fusion 0.240-0.244; all paired bootstrap 95% CIs included zero). Conclusions: Structured EHR data alone matched the discrimination and, after recalibration, the calibration of more complex multimodal fusion for 30-day COPD readmission prediction. These findings highlight the importance of rigorous temporal-leakage auditing in multimodal clinical prediction research and suggest that reformulating this task around temporal proximity to the outcome, rather than refining the fusion mechanism further, may be more productive for future work.

title: Compile What the Environment Decides: Read-Only Speculation and Compiled Procedures for LLM Agents
abstract: An LLM agent pays a model turn for every decision, yet many of its decisions are fixed by what its tools returned, not by what the user said. We make this precise and use it in two regimes. While a user is present, a program learned from traces can take over only reads, speculatively. Because reads leave the state unchanged until the next write, the decision to speculate separates over reads: make each read whose probability of use before the next write exceeds $\delta/(\beta+\delta)$, for a detour's cost $\delta$ and a saved turn's value $\beta$. That probability, not the next-step probability speculative-action systems rank by, is the one to estimate, and counting estimates it with a calibration error of 0.01–0.08 (against 0.06–0.16). In replay across nine frontier agents it never saw, the speculator takes 86% of retail's read-only ceiling, 10 points more than the next-step speculator. Live on τ²-bench, with no model of its own, it cut GLM-5.3's LLM turns by 28% (95% CI 19–36%) and, in a pre-registered run of three trials, Claude Sonnet 5's by 21% (17–24%) and Claude Haiku 4.5's by 22% (16–29%), with passes no lower. Run live in AgentDojo's own environment with GLM-5.3 and Claude Haiku 4.5, it cut LLM turns by 10% (6–14%) in the suites where the replay found reads to take, with passes unchanged. Where no user speaks, a whole procedure, writes included, can be compiled once: on τ²-bench's solo telecom tasks, a cascade that hands a model only what the procedure's outcome check cannot confirm passes 39 of 40 held-out tasks at 0.48 LLM turns per ticket, against 15.9 for the model alone. Both run in Hoist, an open-source MCP proxy and procedure runtime that serves any agent and any MCP server.

Because reads leave the state unchanged until the next write, the decision to speculate separates over reads: make each read whose probability of use before the next write exceeds $\delta/(\beta+\delta)$, for a detour's cost $\delta$ and a saved turn's value $\beta$. That probability, not the next-step probability speculative-action systems rank by, is the one to estimate, and counting estimates it with a calibration error of 0.01–0.08 (against 0.06–0.16). In replay across nine frontier agents it never saw, the speculator takes 86% of retail's read-only ceiling, 10 points more than the next-step speculator. Live on τ²-bench, with no model of its own, it cut GLM-5.3's LLM turns by 28% (95% CI 19–36%) and, in a pre-registered run of three trials, Claude Sonnet 5's by 21% (17–24%) and Claude Haiku 4.5's by 22% (16–29%), with passes no lower. Run live in AgentDojo's own environment with GLM-5.3 and Claude Haiku 4.5, it cut LLM turns by 10% (6–14%) in the suites where the replay found reads to take, with passes unchanged. Where no user speaks, a whole procedure, writes included, can be compiled once: on τ²-bench's solo telecom tasks, a cascade that hands a model only what the procedure's outcome check cannot confirm passes 39 of 40 held-out tasks at 0.48 LLM turns per ticket, against 15.9 for the model alone. Both run in Hoist, an open-source MCP proxy and procedure runtime that serves any agent and any MCP server.

title: QEC Invariant Compendium: Baseline Equivalence, Trace-Indexed Reuse, Decoder Pipelines, and Dark-State Observables
abstract: This compendium presents four revised studies of deterministic computation, reusable intermediate results, and transformation invariants in belief-propagation diagnostics and quantum error-correction software. It connects earlier QSOL-IMC preprints with commit-pinned QEC source snapshots, reproducible experiments, and machine-checked mathematical models. The four studies examine baseline equivalence between min-sum decoding and unit-weight uniformly reweighted belief propagation; trace-indexed reuse of sign vectors and CRC32 values; the interaction of clipping, damping, freezing, and ternary projection in decoder transformation pipelines; and the interpretation of local “dark-state” observables in belief-propagation traces. The deposit contains four revised papers, editable manuscript sources, a dependency-free Lean 4 project, source snapshots, validation scripts, measured results, proof logs, provenance records, and integrity manifests. The formalization comprises 43 compiled theorem declarations. Empirical validation includes 576 paired decoder cases, 80 cached-versus-inline diagnostic comparisons, a reproduced reduction from 81 to 20 sign computations, 204 selected historical tests, and 18 synthetic dark-state scenario runs. The analysis also documents counterexamples and boundary conditions involving CRC32 collisions, cache provenance, source mutation, damping, NaN handling, transformation order, and the distinction between observed local stability and safe computational reuse. The Lean proofs establish properties of the stated exact mathematical models. They do not constitute a complete refinement proof for the Python/NumPy implementations or IEEE-754 arithmetic, nor do they establish physical quantum-hardware correctness or justify skipping live-decoder updates. Historical runtime improvements are identified as previously reported results, separate from the measurements reproduced in this deposit.

title: Deep Learning-Based Japanese Speech Recognition for Robust Organizational Knowledge Capture
abstract: Online Japanese teaching and organizational knowledge management depend on reliable Japanese automatic speech recognition, while existing conformer models perform poorly amid regional dialects, complex phonetics, and background noise. This paper proposes an improved conformer connectionist temporal classification framework with multi-scale acoustic feature enhancement, dialect adaptation layers, bidirectional acoustic-language model fusion, and multi-task training. Tests on 800 hours of standard, mixed-dialect, and noisy speech data and three months of real-scene deployment show the model improves dialect recognition accuracy by nearly 15% and reduces word error rate by 12% under heavy noise, with only 5 milliseconds longer inference latency than the baseline. Separate module tests show each design strengthens noise resistance, dialect adaptability, and long-sentence modeling. The framework balances accuracy and efficiency, supporting real-time oral teaching feedback and structured extraction of implicit enterprise knowledge from voice recordings.

title: ENSEMBLES DE DEEP LEARNING NO DIAGNÓSTICO DE LESÕES ENDOSCÓPICAS
abstract: Lesões gastrointestinais representam um relevante problema de saúde pública, cuja detecção precoce reduz a mortalidade, apesar da subjetividade da análise manual de imagens endoscópicas. Este trabalho propõe o DeepEnsemble-Endo, um ensemble de weighted soft voting com pesos otimizados via grid search. Após avaliar 11 CNNs pré-treinadas por transfer learning e selecionar as cinco melhores (DenseNet121, ResNet50, InceptionV3, MobileNetV2, EfficientNetB2), os pesos foram sistematicamente otimizados, alcançando 96,63% de acurácia e 97,25% de F1-score - superandos ensembles simples da literatura e evidenciando o potencial da abordagem como suporte automatizado à decisão clínica.

title: From Diagnosis to Decision‐Making: AI ‐Driven Triage of Oral Mucosal Lesions Detected on Intraoral Photographs
abstract: BACKGROUND: Managing oral mucosal lesions in general dental practice is challenging, as visually similar conditions may require very different treatments. We developed an AI-based triage system connecting intraoral image analysis with guideline-based treatment recommendations, tested it externally, and compared its performance with clinicians' recommendations. METHODS: YOLOv8 and YOLOv11 were trained on 4079 intraoral photographs to classify 11 oral mucosal lesion types. These were mapped into five treatment tiers defined by urgency and management aim: T1 specialist referral for malignant and high-risk lesions, T2 interdisciplinary referral for specialist-led non-cancer management, T3 risk-adapted surveillance, T4 dental treatment with reassessment, and T5 no treatment. Model performance was compared with two general dentists and four specialists on an internal test set. YOLOv11 was additionally tested on an external dataset. RESULTS: YOLOv11 outperformed YOLOv8 in macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1 score, achieving 0.72, 0.74, and 0.73 respectively. However, 25% of T1 high-risk cases were under-triaged. YOLOv11 significantly outperformed all clinicians, whose F1 scores ranged from 0.33 to 0.69. External performance decreased markedly (F1 score: 0.58), consistent with domain shift. CONCLUSION: Guideline-oriented AI triage is feasible but requires multicentre training for improved generalizability, as well as safety-focused optimization, and prospective user evaluation before clinical use.

title: Jianmu-Q: Bridging Quantum Field Theory and Quantum Hardware with AI Agents
abstract: Quantum computing offers a promising approach to non-perturbative simulations of quantum field theories, particularly for real-time dynamics and systems affected by the sign problem. Yet translating continuum field theories into quantum computations remains a challenging interdisciplinary task. Here we introduce \texttt{Jianmu-Q}, a multi-agent framework that transforms natural-language descriptions of quantum field theories into quantum simulation workflows. Specialized agents handle theoretical formulation, lattice discretization, qubit mapping, and circuit design, while physical consistency checks and independent numerical calculations provide validation throughout the workflow. We benchmark the framework on three field theories of increasing complexity: the $(1+1)$-dimensional Nambu--Jona-Lasinio and Schwinger models, and a $(2+1)$-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory. Across these systems, noiseless quantum-circuit simulations converge toward independent exact-diagonalization and tensor-network results, while selected circuits are executed on IBM quantum hardware, demonstrating an end-to-end, validation-guided approach to quantum simulation of field theories.

title: Transfer Learning in Bandits from Unknown Adaptive Policies: Problem-Dependent Lower and Upper Bounds
abstract: Transfer learning in stochastic multi-armed bandits is typically studied assuming that prior data forms a fixed offline dataset or is generated by a known source. In practice, historical observations come from a previous adaptive decision process whose policy is unknown. We study this setting for bounded rewards in $[0,1]$. Before the online game starts, the learner receives, for each arm $k$, $N'_k$ observations drawn i.i.d.\ from an unknown distribution $ν'_k$, collected by an arbitrary and possibly data-dependent strategy, so the sample sizes $N'_k$ may be random. Source and target means satisfy $|μ_k-μ'_k|<L_k$ for known constants $(L_k)_k$. We derive an asymptotic problem-dependent lower bound and propose KL-UCB-Transfer, which combines online and historical data and achieves logarithmic regret with an improved leading constant whenever $μ'_a<μ_1-L_a$, and recovers the classical KL-UCB guarantee otherwise. Since bounding the source-target discrepancy is often unrealistic, we relax the assumption to the one-sided condition $μ_k-μ'_k<L_k$ and show that logarithmic regret can survive under misspecification, characterizing three regimes ranging from improvement to a degraded logarithmic bound to a loss of guarantee. Simulations illustrate the practical benefits of exploiting process-generated historical data.

title: Quantum Versus Classical Machine Learning for Neuropsychiatric Disorders: A Feature-Matched Multi-Cohort Evaluation
abstract: Resting-state functional connectivity is widely used in machine learning-based classification of neuropsychiatric disorders. Quantum machine learning models have been proposed for functional connectivity data, but few studies have evaluated them under leave-site-out validation or against matched classical models. We compared six quantum model families with classical ones using identical correlation-derived features across four public cohorts (4,308 subjects). Leave-site-out validation was used for the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE I), ADHD-200 (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), and REST-meta-MDD (major depressive disorder) cohorts, while the UCLA Consortium for Neuropsychiatric Phenomics (UCLA-CNP) was evaluated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation. The quantum kernel was statistically indistinguishable from a matched classical kernel across all four cohorts, with the average accuracy difference within 1.4 percentage points at 95% confidence. On ABIDE I, a hybrid quantum convolutional network achieved similar accuracy to its classical counterpart (0.645 vs. 0.641), while a trainable quantum kernel exceeded its classical counterpart by 0.064 in area under the curve (AUC). Quantum convolutional networks also achieved higher AUC than their matched classical networks on this cohort and showed smaller train-test gaps on all four cohorts, without an accuracy gain. Overall, most quantum models matched their classical counterparts, but none consistently outperformed them. This study, among the first quantum evaluations of ABIDE I under leave-site-out validation, provides a feature-matched benchmark of quantum and classical models comprising 284 matched comparisons. We further analyse fidelity-based graph construction and account for the observed quantum-classical parity through effective-dimension and eigenspectrum analyses.

title: Magic state cultivation on a superconducting quantum processor
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires a universal gate set, but the necessary non-Clifford gates represent a significant resource cost for most quantum error correction architectures. Magic state cultivation offers an efficient alternative to resource-intensive distillation protocols; however, testing the proposal's assumptions represents a challenging departure from quantum memory experiments. We present an experimental study of magic state cultivation on a superconducting quantum processor. We implement cultivation, including code-switching into a surface code, and develop a fault-tolerant measurement protocol to bound the magic state fidelity. Cultivation reduces the error by a factor of 40, with a state fidelity of at least 0.9999(1) (retaining 8% of attempts). Our results experimentally establish magic state cultivation as a viable solution to one of quantum computing's most important challenges.

title: Reproducibility package: An experimental comparison of hyperparameter optimization methods for healthcare machine learning
abstract: Code, data and results for the article “An experimental comparison of hyperparameter optimization methods for healthcare machine learning: From grid search to swarm intelligence” (submitted to PLOS ONE). The package compares six hyperparameter optimization strategies (library defaults, grid search, random search, Bayesian optimization with TPE, the Grey Wolf Optimizer and Particle Swarm Optimization) for Random Forest, Support Vector Machine and Logistic Regression on four public clinical datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, with ten paired seeds (720 runs) and a matched-budget experiment. Contents: the benchmark code and experiment notebook; the exact data arrays with SHA-256 checksums and all train/validation/test split indices; all per-seed results; the optimizer traces; scripts that regenerate every table and figure; and check_paper.py, which recomputes all statistics from the raw results and verifies the tables and the numbers stated in the manuscript (run: python check_paper.py; needs Python 3.9+ with numpy and pandas). Code is released under the MIT licence. The four datasets keep the terms of their original sources.

title: Project Pushkalāvatī / Nirgundi: the Sanskrit parser, its data-driven rule compiler and the Sūtram rule-rewrite language (BUILD-0024 to BUILD-0027)
abstract: The integrated research repository for the Sanskrit source inventory (all 3,983 sūtras as data), a data-driven rule compiler, the observed-form bootstrap, the Sūtram rule-rewrite language, the Sanskrit analysis pipeline, Hindawi ports and Romenagri transliteration tooling. This deposit preserves BUILD-0024, BUILD-0025, BUILD-0026 and BUILD-0027 exactly as delivered: each original archive is included byte for byte, the repository history carries one commit per build, and the final tree is BUILD-0026 with the BUILD-0027 results and correction applied. Twenty files that BUILD-0025 and BUILD-0026 dropped in packaging, including the Pages workflow, are restored from BUILD-0024, and the shell scripts are executable again; SEED-NOTE.md records each. Third-party components keep their own licences.

title: Building Trust in AI-Driven Marketing
abstract: This study investigates the mediating role of Green Knowledge Management (GKM) in the relationship between responsible AI marketing practices and customer trust within the Iraqi digital market. Drawing on the Knowledge-Based View (KBV) and sustainability perspectives, the study proposes that organizations can enhance customer trust by integrating environmentally and ethically oriented knowledge processes, including knowledge acquisition, sharing, and application, into their AI-driven marketing practices. A quantitative research design to be employed using a cross-sectional survey targeting digital platform users in Iraq. Data will be analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) to test both direct and indirect relationships.

title: Variational quantum principal component analysis for Hilbert space Gaussian process regression
abstract: Abstract Gaussian processes are widely used probabilistic models for regression and classification tasks. Their flexibility and ability to quantify uncertainties make them well-suited for many applications. However, their applicability to large datasets is limited by the cubic computational time complexity. While reduced-rank methods such as Hilbert space approximations reduce this complexity, scaling to very large datasets remains challenging. Quantum algorithms are promising candidates to further accelerate such computations. Quantum principal component analysis has previously been applied to Hilbert space Gaussian process regression to address this scaling limitation. However, its applicability is limited by the requirement for fault-tolerant quantum hardware. In this work, we present a hybrid quantum-classical model for reduced-rank Gaussian process regression, where we apply a quantum principal component analysis algorithm based on parameterized quantum circuits to Hilbert space Gaussian process regression. In noiseless simulations on a one-dimensional test function, the resulting model reaches a regression accuracy comparable to that of the exact Gaussian process and the classical Hilbert space Gaussian process. The framework uses shallow parameterized circuits and does not require fault-tolerant quantum hardware, which makes it a candidate for noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.

In noiseless simulations on a one-dimensional test function, the resulting model reaches a regression accuracy comparable to that of the exact Gaussian process and the classical Hilbert space Gaussian process. The framework uses shallow parameterized circuits and does not require fault-tolerant quantum hardware, which makes it a candidate for noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.

title: Leveraging Large Language Model Token Probabilities for Literature Review Abstract Filtering
abstract: Grasping the latest knowledge in any field has become increasingly challenging given the rapid pace of modern publishing. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly embedding models and large language models (LLMs), provide promising tools to aid researchers in the filtration and identification of the most relevant literature. However, there is little practical guidance on how to incorporate LLMs into literature reviews, and there are not yet direct comparisons of embedding models versus generative approaches. In this work, we compare these methods using small local LLMs for literature screening on both a simple dataset containing distinct categories and a more complex example with abstracts obtained from the Web of Science. We find that embedding models perform strongly for simple, well-separated queries due to their robustness and computational efficiency. For more complex filtering tasks, generative approaches based on token probabilities can achieve competitive or superior performance, but only when properly calibrated and when token-level outputs are interpreted as continuous scores rather than binary decisions. However, we show these methods are highly sensitive to prompt formulation, token conventions, and threshold selection.

title: Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions
abstract: We present a scalable framework for solving multi-step tasks through a decentralized market of self-interested agents. Prior theoretical work demonstrated that agents organized through sequential auctions can converge to a globally optimal policy in a Markov decision process (MDP), but relied on the restrictive assumption of the existence of perfect clones as a model of perfect competition. In reality, exact clones drive agent profit to zero, violating the natural risk-reward incentives of participants. Conversely, we empirically demonstrate that the opposite extreme, absence of competition, also leads to market failure and value extraction collapse. Between these two extremes, we investigate how heterogeneous agents can survive in markets that span the critical middle ground of imperfect competition. To be profitable, agents learn to strategically shade bids to secure positive individual profit margins, while still ensuring that the marketplace functions effectively enough so that collaborative tasks posed by market consumers can still be solved. We formulate and evaluate four bidding algorithms (Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO) across three auction protocols (1st-Price, 2nd-Price, and Credit-Conserving Vickrey). Across a diverse set of domains, we demonstrate that imperfect competition successfully sustains necessary agent profit margins while maintaining high task success rates at low costs.

title: The Tilted Sampling Problem: Optimism, Posterior Sampling, and Logarithmic Regret
abstract: Many modern learning systems are used not to select a single best action, but to sample diverse high-quality outputs. Examples include entropy-regularized reinforcement learning, RLHF, and reward-guided generative modeling. Motivated by these settings, we study tilted sampling: an online learning problem in which the goal is to sample from the Gibbs distribution induced by an unknown reward function. We define sampling regret as the temperature-normalized cumulative KL divergence between the learner's distribution and the Gibbs target, corresponding to the suboptimality gap in entropy-regularized reward maximization. Our framework generalizes recent sampling-based and KL-regularized formulations in bandits and reinforcement learning. Our main contribution is a general regret framework that captures the different uncertainty structure of tilted sampling and classical regret minimization. While standard regret scales as $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ due to first-order uncertainty, sampling regret is governed by squared confidence widths, yielding logarithmic-in-$T$ regret in standard settings at fixed temperature. We develop sampling analogues of UCB and Thompson sampling (UCS and TS$^2$) and provide unified regret decompositions that explain and extend recent logarithmic guarantees, including the first Bayesian sampling-regret decomposition based on new bounds for posterior-random Gibbs distributions. Our results show that learning to sample from a soft-optimal distribution is statistically distinct from learning to identify a hard optimum.

title: Descending Everest with First-Order Oracles: Oracle Complexity of Convex Optimization under $(L_0,L_1)$-Smoothness
abstract: For convex $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth functions, the curvature may grow together with the gradient norm. Therefore, even when $\|x^0-x^*\|\le R$, the gradient and the optimality gap at the starting point may be exponentially large in $L_1R$, and the bound $\sqrt{L_0R^2/\varepsilon}$, known for the accelerated method on functions with Lipschitz gradient, no longer describes the complexity of the problem. We determine the oracle complexity of this class for arbitrary deterministic first-order methods: for $L_0R^2/\varepsilon\ge1$, the optimal number of oracle calls $N$ satisfies $1+N=\widetildeΘ(\sqrt{L_0R^2/\varepsilon}+L_1R)$. The upper bound reads $O(\sqrt{L_0R^2/\varepsilon}+(1+L_1R)\log(2+L_1R))$: the method first passes through the large-gradient regime in $O(1+L_1R)$ iterations with an inexact line search, and then the standard accelerated method with a constant stepsize takes over. The lower bound is obtained by means of chains and the orthogonal invariance principle on functions conjugate to strongly convex functions on a polytope. If the initial optimality gap is at most $4\varepsilon$, the optimal bound becomes $1+N=\widetildeΘ(\sqrt{L_0R^2/\varepsilon}+(L_1R)^{2/3})$.

title: Online Quantile Omniprediction for Proper Losses
abstract: The task of constructing a predictor that is simultaneously accurate under multiple evaluation metrics has been popularized recently under the name omniprediction. Prior work in this area has largely focused on binary prediction tasks, and existing results for multiclass and continuous outcomes typically suffer from slow error rates. In this paper, we consider forecasts expressed as a set of quantiles over a discrete but otherwise arbitrary set of probability levels. We develop sample-efficient algorithms for constructing forecasts that are accurate simultaneously across all proper losses that satisfy mild regularity conditions, where proper losses are those minimized by predicting the true quantiles. Our algorithms are online and can operate in a dynamic environment, while simultaneously taking multiple losses into account, and their forecasts offer the potential to provide diverse end-users with rich information for evaluating risk and informing a range of practical decision-making tasks. As an example, we demonstrate how our procedure can be used to ensemble quantile forecasts of COVID-19 hospitalizations made by experts during the pandemic.

title: Noise-Space Reward Alignment for Few-Step Generative Models
abstract: Few-step generative models produce high-quality samples in one or a few evaluations. However, steering them toward desired properties remains difficult, especially when only black-box reward evaluations are available. While one could apply approaches developed for iterative diffusion and flow-based models, such as direct RL fine-tuning or test-time scaling, we find that neither transfers well to the few-step regime: direct fine-tuning suffers from severe reward over-optimization, and test-time scaling sacrifices the efficiency advantage of few-step generation. We propose Noise Policy Optimization (NPO), which explicitly targets the alignment problem for few-step generative models. The key idea is to learn an amortized flow policy over the initial noise space of the generator. The trained policy transports Gaussian noise to a reward-tilted noise distribution, whose pushforward distribution through the frozen generator is exactly the reward-tilted output distribution. By keeping the generator frozen, we can effectively utilize the knowledge encoded in the pretrained model, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning. The amortized policy moves the search cost into training, so inference adds only a lightweight noise sampling step on top of the pretrained model. To improve sample efficiency during training, we use ELBO-based likelihood estimation that requires only sampled endpoints rather than simulated trajectories. Across image, language, and protein structure generation, NPO consistently achieves a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning, and matches test-time search methods with 16 to 549 times lower inference cost.

title: Compression-Based Linguistic Complexity Metrics in Automatic Essay Scoring
abstract: Compression-based linguistic complexity metrics enable cross-linguistic comparison without prior annotation. Their sensitivity to variation across languages and Portuguese registers highlights their applicability in NLP tasks. This study investigates their use as readability proxies and complementary features in Automatic Essay Scoring. We analyze how these metrics capture variation in essay quality across traits, genres, and educational levels in Brazilian Portuguese. In addition, we evaluate their sensitivity to differences between humanand AI-generated essays. Our results suggest that complexity metrics are effective (i) in differentiating educational levels, (ii) in detecting whether they were written by humans and (iii) as predictors of essay quality.

title: Symmetric weighing matrices SW(25,16), SW(27,16) and SW(29,16)
abstract: We exhibit symmetric weighing matrices SW(25,16), SW(27,16) and SW(29,16), i.e. symmetric n×n matrices W with entries in {0,±1} and WWT = 16I for n = 25, 27, 29. These three orders were listed as the remaining open instances for weight 16 in recent literature (Rosin, arXiv:2505.23881; arXiv:2501.17725, Table 2). Each matrix was found by a SAT search in which a signed-permutation automorphism of a chosen cycle type was prescribed. Existence is established by the explicit certificates, which are printed in the appendix of the note and supplied as plain-text files (a second, different SW(27,16) is included); each was checked by two independently written exact-integer programs. To verify any matrix in seconds: python3 check_sw_int.py SW_27_16.txt 27 16 (pure Python, no dependencies; prints VALID and exits 0). Provenance: the searches were planned and run by an AI agent (agent-afk) under the author's supervision.

title: Phaneia Evaluation Methodology for AI Agents
abstract: This document defines how Phaneia GmbH evaluates whether an AI agent or agentic system does something it must not when an adversary controls part of its inputs: content it reads, its configuration, or messages from other agents. Every trial is scored deterministically against evidence the agent did not produce: what the systems it acts on actually recorded, compared with obligations defined outside the agent. No language model sits in the scoring path. The methodology covers: access tiers and environment fidelity; scenario families and trial design, with attack and baseline arms of at least 30 trials; two complementary checks (obligation-detection and claim-verification), and statistical reporting with Fisher exact tests and Wilson intervals; instrument validation; the content and validity of the evaluation letter; re-evaluations and repeat runs; independence rules, versioning and limitations. It builds on Schwyzer (2026), Adversarial Assessment of Agentic Systems (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23043956). Payloads, attack chains and the scenario library are not part of this public document. Reports and evaluation letters cite the version DOI of the methodology they were produced under.

title: VTutor Pro VZona v10.6.5 STABLE: AI-Assisted Conversational Tutoring with Institutional Mini-RAG for Moodle
abstract: VTutor Pro VZona v10.6.5 STABLE — Institutional Mini-RAG for Moodle VTutor Pro VZona es un componente de software educativo para Moodle 4.5+, desarrollado para apoyar procesos de tutoría conversacional mediante inteligencia artificial generativa y recuperación documental contextualizada. La versión 10.6.5 STABLE (build 2026082406) integra un Mini-RAG institucional con recuperación semántica, mecanismos de respaldo léxico, aislamiento contextual por curso y permisos de usuario, trazabilidad documental y herramientas de diagnóstico READ-ONLY. El proceso de desarrollo se documenta desde la perspectiva de Design Science Research (DSR), mediante iteraciones de construcción, revisión técnica, pruebas funcionales y decisiones de estabilización. La versión publicada corresponde a la promoción de FINAL QA6 (build 2026082405) a STABLE (build 2026082406). La comparación estática de ambos paquetes identificó modificaciones de metadatos, documentación y actualización, sin cambios en la lógica principal de recuperación y enrutamiento. Alcance de la evidencia: Las verificaciones documentadas respaldan la integridad y características técnicas examinadas. No constituyen evidencia experimental de mejoras en el aprendizaje, eficacia pedagógica ni validación independiente de seguridad o rendimiento. title: GeoRacoon: A Python package for scalable, parallelized geospatial raster analysis
abstract: GeoRacoon is aimed at supporting work and analyses with large spatial raster data. It heavily relies on RasterIO (rio) extending its functionality and usability. Leveraging GDAL's block-based read/write capability, GeoRacoon implements efficient multi-core support (i.e. parallelization) for various high and low-level operations, such as convolution operations (e.g., applying a Gaussian filter) or even area-wide multiple linear regressions. It also facilitates GeoTIFF handling with an object oriented abstraction layer to RasterIO which incorporates the management of metadata with source and band tagging. GeoRacoon provides 3 packages, riogrande, convster, coonfit, which facilitate (in our opinion) working with TIFF files. RioGrande is the great heart of the GeoRacoon and adds functionality for parallel processing using block-based I/O, dataset compatibility checks, data type conversion, mask and selector creation as well as simple file compression. Convster allows for (Gaussian) convolution of raster files using parallelized processing, coon-style. While Gaussian and border-preserving Gaussian filters are default parameters, other filters can be used. CoonFit allows to fit linear models the coon-way, meaning parallelized and fast, while understandable due to the reliance on matrix operations

title: Adversarial Robustness of Deep Learning–Based Network Intrusion Detection Under Encrypted Traffic
abstract: The deployment of encryption protocols, such as TLS 1.3, QUIC, Encrypted Client Hello and DNS-over-HTTPS, has compelled deep learning-based network intrusion detection systems (DL-NIDS) to rely on metadata for classification. This chapter explores adversarial robustness issues and challenges of DL-NIDS on encrypted traffic. Contrary to adversarial machine learning that assumes a common feature space to which attacks are defined, encrypted metadata has heterogenous, protocol-constrained features: packet sizes constrained by transmission unit sizes, timing features constrained by latency budgets, and nominal handshake features constrained by candidate lists. This chapter defines metadata-specific adversarial models, identifies protocol-valid evasion and poisoning attacks, studies countermeasures in constrained feature spaces, and proposes protocol-aligned evaluation for DL-NIDS. By developing perturbation models for encrypted and non-encrypted traffic, this chapter lays the groundwork for developing secure DL-NIDS in an encrypted future.

title: Event Log Behavioral Privacy Protection Method Based on Relaxed Behavioral Profiles
abstract: Privacy preservation techniques for event logs prevent sensitive information leakage by injecting noise into log data, thus mitigating privacy risks in business process management. While ensuring privacy, this approach often reduces data utility and impacts subsequent analysis accuracy. Current research mainly optimizes noise injection based on data attributes to preserve utility, but overlooks how behavioral relationship changes affect data quality. To address this, this paper proposes a privacy protection method for event logs based on relaxed behavioral profiles. First, a behavioral privacy attack model is formalized to reveal how behavioral relationships can lead to privacy leakage. Building on this, data attributes are utilized to extend behavioral profiles, and a behavioral profile extension algorithm is proposed to analyze implicit behavioral relationships between activities. This allows building a multi-perspective perturbation set combining behavioral and data attributes. Finally, perturbations are injected using differential privacy methods. Experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that the event logs generated by this method are behavior-unchanged at the level of the modeled relations, effectively mitigating the utility loss caused by log anonymization and attaining F1-scores of up to 0.874 on synthetic data, comparable to those of the baselines.

title: DEEP LEARNING ENSEMBLES FOR THE DIAGNOSIS OF ENDOSCOPIC LESIONS
authors: Luiz Otávio de Oliveira Souza Júnior
abstract: Gastrointestinal lesions represent a significant public health concern, where early detection reduces mortality despite the subjectivity of manual endoscopic image analysis. This work proposes DeepEnsemble-Endo, a weighted soft voting ensemble with weights optimized via grid search. After evaluating 11 pre-trained CNNs via transfer learning and selecting the top-5 (DenseNet121, ResNet50, InceptionV3, MobileNetV2, EfficientNetB2), weights were systematically optimized, achieving 96.63% accuracy and 97.25% F1-score - outperforming simple ensembles from the literature and demonstrating potential as automated clinical decision support.

title: Quantisation Costs More in Greek than in English, Cybersecurity Knowledge of Small Local Language Models
abstract: Small open language models that run on an ordinary office computer are an attractive basis for a security awareness assistant, and platforms such as SentinelSphere ship one in a compressed quantised form, that stores the numbers inside the model with fewer bits. This study asks how much cybersecurity knowledge this compression costs, and whether the cost is larger in Greek than in English. A sample of questions from the CyberMetric benchmark was translated into Greek with an open translation model that was not itself tested, the translation was checked by translating it back, and the same questions were put in both languages to Phi-4-mini at three levels of compression, to the general model Qwen2.5-3B and to the Greek adapted model Krikri-8B, all on a two core processor. Phi-4-mini answers Greek questions clearly worse than English ones even with light compression. The four bit compression that platforms ship costs almost nothing in English but a clear share of accuracy in Greek, and the strongest compression brings Greek close to guessing while English stays usable. The general model is the most accurate in English but among the weakest in Greek, where it needs about four times as many text pieces per question, while the Greek adapted model keeps the gap smallest at the price of a larger and slower file. Files made without the calibration step that relies on mostly English text, including the file the platform publishes, lose the same Greek accuracy at four bits. A compression level found acceptable in English should therefore not be assumed acceptable in Greek.

title: Gradient-Hessian Query Tradeoffs: Matching Lower Bounds in Logarithmic Dimension
abstract: We establish matching lower bounds for the tradeoff between gradient and Hessian queries in nonconvex optimization with Lipschitz Hessian. In normalized units, the initial objective gap is at most $T$, the Hessian Lipschitz constant is at most one, and the target gradient norm is one. For sufficiently large $T$, dimension $d \ge C\log(2+T)$, and a prescribed Hessian budget $h \ge 1$ with $h+1 \le aT$, every randomized algorithm requires $Ω(\min\{Td^{1/3}, T^{3/2}/\sqrt{h+1}\})$ ordinary queries. An ordinary query returns the value and gradient; a Hessian query returns the complete second jet and is charged only to its own budget. Both budgets are worst-case caps. Queries and outputs may be arbitrary real points, and no Hessian-norm bound is imposed. The hard input law consists of fixed, globally $C^3$, coercive functions. The construction combines sequential readouts of a continuous random matrix with localized completion blocks and reliability dimensions that vary across hierarchy levels. Premature disclosures are charged by their expected task cost, while every oracle reply remains the exact jet of the presampled objective. This yields a logarithmic dimension threshold and a depth-independent third-derivative bound. Together with a translation of the NALEN upper bound of Chen, Liu, Luo, and Zhang, the result determines the query tradeoff up to absolute constants throughout the stated range.
