title: Seeing is Believing: Benchmarking and Mitigating the Interference of Language Priors on Visual Perception in MLLMs
abstract: Language priors in MLLMs can override visual evidence, impairing visual perception. Existing benchmarks assume shared priors across models and rely solely on accuracy. However, cross-model prior agreement falls below 80%, and over 15% of items can be answered correctly without any image, causing accuracy to overestimate prior resistance. To address these limitations, we introduce ViSiP-Bench, a benchmark grounded in rare-but-real scenarios across six prior categories, with a model-aware dynamic prior induction protocol and three metrics that more precisely and continuously measure prior resistance than accuracy alone. Evaluating 24 models reveals that prior adherence is pervasive, does not improve with scale, and larger models tend to either strongly override their priors or firmly adhere to them. We therefore propose MAPS, which identifies each model's strongest priors and fine-tunes on factually grounded knowledge to soften excessive prior reliance without disrupting general capabilities.

title: Learning to Search for Executable Patternmaking from Certified Programs
abstract: Recent models generate sewing patterns from images or text, and program-based representations make these patterns executable. These systems produce a finished pattern and do not model how a patternmaker turns one pattern into another. In practice a new style is made by editing an existing pattern: lengthening the bodice, moving a dart, swapping a sleeve. Pattern archives record the results of such edits and none of the steps. We observe that the steps can be recovered by searching over editing actions until one pattern becomes the other. A deterministic compiler makes the recovered steps checkable. To this end, we present SemDraft, the first framework that learns to search for executable patternmaking programs from paired before-and-after sewing patterns without recorded editing steps. Specifically, a bounded search recovers a program of editing actions and certifies it only after three checks: it recompiles from scratch, every pair of its actions is classified as ordered or interchangeable, and an independent replay reaches the same pattern. The certified programs then train a model that ranks candidate actions inside the same search. On two frozen draws of 80 order-sensitive cases, with every other search component fixed, the learned ranker certifies 63 and 64 cases within 1,000 search executions, against at most 53 and 52 for non-learned rankers.

title: DST-Net: Decomposed Spatio-Temporal Network for Time Series Forecasting
abstract: Series decomposition has emerged as a widely acknowledged paradigm in deep time series forecasting models. However, existing approaches predominantly employ a homogeneous modeling strategy for all subsequences, thereby overlooking the distinct inductive biases inherent in different components. We identify that the trend component exhibits dominant spatial coupling across channels but carries significant temporal redundancy, whereas the seasonal component is characterized by local temporal evolution but remains susceptible to attention distraction. To address this, we propose a novel disentangled architecture that tailors specific modeling strategies to align with the intrinsic properties of each component. For the trend branch, we design a Latent Graph Block, employing latent graph modeling to capture global topological dependencies and system-wide co-movements. Conversely, for the seasonal branch, we introduce a Gaussian Multi-scale Attention mechanism to mitigate attention distraction. By injecting learnable Gaussian priors, we impose structural constraints that compel the model to focus on multi-granular local contexts, effectively filtering out global noise and accurately capturing local evolutionary phases. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model.

title: Interpolation of unitaries with time-dependent Hamiltonians via Deep Learning
abstract: Abstract Quantum systems governed by time-dependent Hamiltonians pose significant challenges for the accurate computation of unitary time-evolution operators, which are essential for predicting quantum state dynamics. In this work, we introduce a physics-informed deep learning approach based on Physics-Informed Neural Networks to estimate these operators over the full time domain. By incorporating physical constraints such as unitarity and leveraging the second-order Magnus expansion or Trotterization on the evolution operator, the proposed framework enables the estimation of unitary matrices at different time intervals. The model is trained using simulated unitary operators and evaluated on quantum systems ranging from 2 to 6 qubits, governed by a fully non-zero Pauli Hamiltonian. For larger many-body systems, specifically those with 7 and 8 qubits, the same methodology is employed to reconstruct an effective time-dependent Hamiltonian, restricted to nearest-neighbor Ising and XYZ Heisenberg models, from which the corresponding time-evolution operator is computed over the entire temporal domain. Across all system sizes, the framework achieves high gate fidelities using a limited number of unitary samples, with a statistical analysis over independent Hamiltonian realizations confirming mean fidelities close to 0.99 and low variability. Furthermore, once trained, the model interpolates the evolution operator with inference times substantially lower than those of a numerical interpolation baseline, indicating a potential reduction in measurement and data acquisition costs. These results highlight the effectiveness of the approach for data-driven simulation and identification of quantum dynamical systems, with direct relevance to quantum computing and quantum simulation applications.

title: Evaluating Portuguese Tokenizers as Morpheme Sequence in Relation to LLM Downstream Performance
abstract: Sub-word tokenizers allow us to handle open vocabulary problems using a relatively small set of tokens. Despite its ease of use, it usually relies on a data-driven approach that does not directly employ linguistic or morphologic features for text tokenization. [Bostrom and Durrett 2020] and [Hofmann et al. 2021] demonstrate that morphemes improve LLM performance on English texts. In this work, we explore the hypothesis that tokenizers that are capable of producing a token sequence better aligned with a morpheme sequence can improve LLMs performance on Brazilian Portuguese. To evaluate how the presence of morphemes can impact LLMs for Brazilian Portuguese, we propose MorphEval-PT, a new evaluation procedure based on the psycholinguistic concept of morphological models of word processing. We build new BPE and Unigram vocabularies that are evaluated on MorphEval-PT and, in order to validate the impact of morphemes on LLMs performance, train new LLMs from scratch and evaluate its performance on downstream tasks. Consistently, BPE demonstrates a higher precision score than Unigram in its ability to represent morphemes, as well as better performance on every downstream task. These promising results indicate that accessing the ability of tokenizers to represent morphemes is an important feature in the development of LLMs for Brazilian Portuguese and that MorphEval-PT is a good and lightweight method to improve LLM performance before any pre-training.

title: Garbage Collecting the External Effects of AI Agents
abstract: AI agents open pull requests, allocate cloud resources, charge cards, and post status updates to team channels. They increasingly delegate their work to trees of sub-agents and helper processes that the model shapes at runtime. When these computations end before their work is done, for example because the user cancels them, their token budget runs out, or they crash, their processes stop, but their effects remain. We argue that managing these effects is a garbage collection problem over external services. Remove an effect too early, and something that depends on it breaks. Never remove it, and it leaks. Unlike memory, this heap belongs to other services, the code that creates effects is chosen at runtime and cannot be instrumented, other people start depending on effects without telling anyone, and every part of the system can crash. We present effect recovery, an abstraction for disposing of the external effects a computation leaves behind when it ends. It guarantees that a computation leaves no dangling effects and no silent leaks. It records every effect before it happens and decides what happens to each one after the computation ends. Requests leave the computation only through a monitor, which records each one before forwarding it. Because the computation can stop at any point, a controller that outlives it works from this record. It removes an effect only when removal is known to be safe, and otherwise keeps it or escalates it to a human. Effects that no later step needs, such as the final pull request, wait until the user completes the task, so an aborted task never creates them. Our evaluation shows that our implementation of effect recovery mediates real agent workloads without meaningfully reducing their task success or adding noticeable latency, and that its guarantee holds when computations fail at any point.

title: Beyond Pairwise Accuracy: Testing Synthetic Manufacturing Data
abstract: This Jupyter Notebook investigates whether synthetic quality-control records preserve a manufacturing relationship defined by XOR. Using two fictional datasets with identical one-way and two-way distributions but different three-way structures, it compares pairwise and full-joint OpenDP measurements fitted with Private-PGM, alongside an MST demonstration. Repeated experiments measure marginal accuracy, defect prevalence, XOR agreement and synthetic sampling error. Tables, plots and a data-driven interpretation explain the findings, privacy accounting and implications for sharing manufacturing data.

title: From "Computational Problem-Solving" to "Question Emergence": On the Intrinsic Boundary of Al Mathematical Research and the Ultimate Defense of Human Cognition
abstract: Recently, Al has concentrated on solving a large number of unsolved problems in mathematics with its powerful computational capacity, sparking widespread attention in both academia and industry. Some views hold that Al will rapidly replace mathematicians, and by extension, gradually replace physicists and all engineering professionals. This paper dissects this "computational replacement theory" through logical reductio ad absurdum. It points out that machine-style problem-solving can produce correct "results, " yet it cannot "emerge new disciplines and fields in the process of solving major problems as humans do. Current Al technology is essentially confined to three closed technical paths: "brute-force enumeration, internal optimization within closed systems, and probability theory." It lacks the "conceptual isolation" and "practicality" core that are crucial to human cognition. Therefore, Al cannot truly replace the subject position of humanity in scientific exploration. Keywords: Computational problem-solving; Question emergence; Conceptual isolation; Practicality; Intrinsic boundary;Human originality

title: Orb GraphRAG pipeline study: raw results and model-call cache (September-October 2026)
abstract: Every run, log and recorded model call from a four-week study (18 September to 14 October 2026) of the local question-answering pipeline of Orb, a desktop notes app that builds a knowledge graph from your notes. Ten rounds on HotpotQA and MuSiQue tested extraction models (Gemma 4, Qwen 3.5, Phi-4, Granite 4.2), retrieval strategies (raw passages, keyword search, PageRank expansion, evidence ordering), answering models, and a reranker scoring fix. Contents: llm-cache/ holds 76,023 recorded model calls, content-addressed, which replay every run without a GPU. machines/ holds each GPU machine's per-question results with full traces, run configurations, index-build records and logs. The README maps folders to rounds. Code, reports and the lab notebook: branch orb-testing of github.com/josetseph/Orb (commit b4e51c0). Notes are passages from HotpotQA (CC BY-SA 4.0) and MuSiQue (CC BY 4.0), derived from Wikipedia. The bundle is one tar.gz split into six parts. Rebuild with cat orb-research-data.tar.gz.part-* > orb-research-data.tar.gz (md5 5526e60e3817f3fabd46f8e9d78bd243). The same data is browsable at https://huggingface.co/datasets/josetseph/orb-graphrag-study.

title: Special issue on trustworthy and safe AI: Interpretability, robustness, and security
abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly in large language models (LLMs) and physical robotics, have rapidly reshaped daily life and industrial applications.As these systems become more capable and autonomous, ensuring their safety, trustworthiness, robustness, and alignment with human values has become increasingly important.In response to these challenges, this special issue on "Trustworthy and Safe AI: Interpretability, Robustness, and Security" brings together recent research that advances the safety and trustworthiness of AI across diverse models, systems, and real-world applications.This special issue received 50 submissions, reflecting the growing research interest in trustworthy and safe AI.Following a rigorous peer-review process, 11 papers were selected for publication.Together, these studies span several interconnected dimensions of the field, ranging from emerging security threats in LLMs and multiagent systems to robustness, autonomous system safety, and explainability for practical deployment.The following five papers focus on emerging security and safety threats across modern AI systems.These studies examine how vulnerabilities arise from adversarial attacks, multi-agent interactions, social context, multilingual settings, and hidden information while exploring the corresponding mechanisms for detection and defense.In [1], the authors investigate a more evasive mixed clean/dirty-label X-to-X backdoor attack and propose an ensemble defense that combines complementary detectors such as Neural Cleanse, PT-RED, CEPA, and MMBD.This work is significant because it addresses both robustness and interpretability, and the ensemble improves resilience across diverse backdoor mechanisms while also supporting trigger inversion to help explain the nature of the detected attack.By jointly considering stronger adversarial attacks, generalized defense, and interpretable backdoor analysis, this study aligns well with the themes of Trustworthy and Safe AI: Interpretability, Robustness, and Security.In [2], the authors study how a single malicious agent can compromise the collective decision-making of otherwise well-aligned LLM agents in a collaborative financial multi-agent environment and proposes a datalineage-based systemic defense.Its main contribution is to show that the interaction dynamics themselves can become a security vulnerability, extending AI safety concerns beyond isolated models to multi-agent societies.By analyzing poisoning, social conformity, and system-level verification across multiple models and network settings, this study offers timely insights into the robustness, safety, and trustworthy coordination of emerging autonomous multi-agent AI systems.The paper [3] titled "Lost in the comments: Social context as a single-pass jailbreak and defense on agentic platforms" by Jeongsu Park and colleagues investigates how comments, reactions, and engagement signals surrounding harmful content influence the safety behavior of LLMs in agentic social platforms.The study demonstrates that the ambient social context, even without explicit malicious instructions, can substantially alter attack success rates, whereas ethically framed comments can reinforce safe behavior through the same contextual channel.Through controlled experiments that varied the valence, volume, and engagement of social signals, this study shows that the nature of the surrounding commentary is more important than its quantity in determining whether model safety is weakened or strengthened.This work is particularly valuable because it extends indirect prompt-injection research to the emerging setting of multi-agent platforms and provides evidence that social context can function as both an attack mechanism and a potential defensive control.Supported by comparisons with PAIR, independent rescoring with WildGuard, human adjudication, and signal-separation ablation

evidence.title: Special issue on trustworthy and safe AI: Interpretability, robustness, and security
evidence.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly in large language models (LLMs) and physical robotics, have rapidly reshaped daily life and industrial applications.As these systems become more capable and autonomous, ensuring their safety, trustworthiness, robustness, and alignment with human values has become increasingly important.In response to these challenges, this special issue on "Trustworthy and Safe AI: Interpretability, Robustness, and Security" brings together recent research that advances the safety and trustworthiness of AI across diverse models, systems, and real-world applications.This special issue received 50 submissions, reflecting the growing research interest in trustworthy and safe AI.Following a rigorous peer-review process, 11 papers were selected for publication.Together, these studies span several interconnected dimensions of the field, ranging from emerging security threats in LLMs and multiagent systems to robustness, autonomous system safety, and explainability for practical deployment.The following five papers focus on emerging security and safety threats across modern AI systems.These studies examine how vulnerabilities arise from adversarial attacks, multi-agent interactions, social context, multilingual settings, and hidden information while exploring the corresponding mechanisms for detection and defense.In [1], the authors investigate a more evasive mixed clean/dirty-label X-to-X backdoor attack and propose an ensemble defense that combines complementary detectors such as Neural Cleanse, PT-RED, CEPA, and MMBD.This work is significant because it addresses both robustness and interpretability, and the ensemble improves resilience across diverse backdoor mechanisms while also supporting trigger inversion to help explain the nature of the detected attack.By jointly considering stronger adversarial attacks, generalized defense, and interpretable backdoor analysis, this study aligns well with the themes of Trustworthy and Safe AI: Interpretability, Robustness, and Security.In [2], the authors study how a single malicious agent can compromise the collective decision-making of otherwise well-aligned LLM agents in a collaborative financial multi-agent environment and proposes a datalineage-based systemic defense.Its main contribution is to show that the interaction dynamics themselves can become a security vulnerability, extending AI safety concerns beyond isolated models to multi-agent societies.By analyzing poisoning, social conformity, and system-level verification across multiple models and network settings, this study offers timely insights into the robustness, safety, and trustworthy coordination of emerging autonomous multi-agent AI systems.The paper [3] titled "Lost in the comments: Social context as a single-pass jailbreak and defense on agentic platforms" by Jeongsu Park and colleagues investigates how comments, reactions, and engagement signals surrounding harmful content influence the safety behavior of LLMs in agentic social platforms.The study demonstrates that the ambient social context, even without explicit malicious instructions, can substantially alter attack success rates, whereas ethically framed comments can reinforce safe behavior through the same contextual channel.Through controlled experiments that varied the valence, volume, and engagement of social signals, this study shows that the nature of the surrounding commentary is more important than its quantity in determining whether model safety is weakened or strengthened.This work is particularly valuable because it extends indirect prompt-injection research to the emerging setting of multi-agent platforms and provides evidence that social context can function as both an attack mechanism and a potential defensive control.Supported by comparisons with PAIR, independent rescoring with WildGuard, human adjudication, and signal-separation ablation

title: When the Image Lies
abstract: Generative systems can now synthesize moving images that are indistinguishable from footage captured by a camera. In doing so, they quietly dismantle two assumptions on which law has long depended: that a video is recorded by someone, and that it shows something that actually occurred. This chapter examines the consequences of that dismantling along three fault lines. The first is authorship, where the requirement of human creativity leaves fully machine-generated video in an uneasy ownership vacuum. The second is accountability, where responsibility for a harmful fabrication is spread thinly across model developers, platforms, deployers, and end users. The third is legal uncertainty, expressed in a fast-growing but fragmented body of statutes, transparency mandates. The chapter argues that the core problem is not a single doctrinal gap but a mismatch between an evidentiary culture inherited from photography and a technology that severs the image from its origin. It proposes a governance response on content provenance, graduated liability, evidentiary reform, and media literacy.

title: ResStreamGS: Residual-Sensitive Dual-Stream Gaussian Splatting for Mobile Volumetric Video Streaming
abstract: Real-time mobile volumetric video enables immersive free-viewpoint experiences, but delivering high-quality 3D content under constrained bandwidth and computation remains challenging. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) systems, such as V$^3$, enable efficient mobile streaming by encoding time-varying Gaussian attributes with commodity video codecs and hardware decoding. However, existing pipelines treat all Gaussians as frame-varying signals, which is poorly suited to full-scene content where large portions remain temporally stable. Our empirical study shows that frame-wise adaptation and video coding of all Gaussians cause quality degradation in complex full-scene content, particularly in temporally stable regions. To address this issue, we propose ResStreamGS, a residual-sensitive dual-stream framework that processes Gaussians according to their temporal behavior. ResStreamGS identifies residual-sensitive primitives through lightweight probe adaptation and reuses stable Gaussians within each Group of Pictures (GOP). Stable Gaussians are transmitted once per GOP, while only residual-sensitive Gaussians remain in the frame-wise hardware-decodable video stream. Experiments on complex full-scene volumetric videos show that ResStreamGS improves post-codec PSNR by 7.51--8.35~dB over a controlled V$^3$-style all-Gaussians baseline, reduces amortized payload by up to 56.5%, and achieves 30.883~FPS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 778G platform.

title: Construction and decoding of convolutional codes with optimal column distances
abstract: The construction of Maximum Distance Profile (MDP) convolutional codes in general requires the use of very large finite fields. In contrast, convolutional codes with optimal column distances maximize the column distances for given code parameters $ (n, k, \delta) $ and a given arbitrary finite field. In this paper, we present a construction of such convolutional codes. In addition, we prove that for the considered parameters the codes that we constructed are the only ones achieving optimal column distances. The structure of the presented convolutional codes with optimal column distances is strongly related to first order Reed-Muller block codes and we leverage this fact to develop a reduced complexity version of the Viterbi algorithm for these codes.

title: Demonstration of RDF and SPARQL 1.2 Interoperability through Query Rewriting
abstract: With the finalization of rdf 1.2 and sparql 1.2, the new triple-term construct brings native reification to rdf. native support, however, does not imply uniform adoption: existing datasets continue to model statement-level metadata through established reification patterns, so federated queries must mediate between these patterns and the new syntax. we address this by rewriting queries written against triple terms into queries over the reification pattern actually used by each source, expressing the relationship as a sparql construct query that is unfolded into the user’s query. this paper demonstrates the approach through a web interface in which users author their own mappings, select sources, and observe how their queries are rewritten and executed across federated endpoints. reification translation is one application of a more general framework for sparql query answering under declarative rdf-to-rdf mappings, which we plan to formalize and optimize. the language gaps it exposes also give us concrete input for the upcoming sparql maintenance-mode standardization.

title: Data and code for "The gross code's depth-8 syndrome cycle has circuit distance 10"
abstract: Code, SAT formulas, DRAT proofs (607), logs, Stim circuits and fault sets for the paper. They support proofs that the depth-8 syndrome cycle of Bravyi et al. has circuit distance 6, 8, 8 and 10 for the [[72,12,6]], [[90,8,10]], [[108,8,10]] and [[144,12,12]] codes for every number of cycles; a comparison with Google's Tesseract test circuits; and independent confirmations for the [[360,12]] code and the left-right gross-code circuit. See README.md.

title: Site adaptation of CAMS without a local station in West Africa: transfer cost and bias structure
abstract: Ground measurements of solar irradiance are scarce in West Africa, and most sites have no station with which to adapt satellite estimates. A CAMS site adaptation learned at existing stations can instead be transferred to such a site. The cost of this transfer is evaluated at 31 West African stations, with corrections learned on one year of data and tested on the following year. For global horizontal irradiance (GHI), having no local measurement adds about one percentage point to the mean absolute error of the annual total. The north–south trend in the bias transfers, but each station retains an offset of its own. Part of the observed excess error comes from the sensors. With independent calibration errors of 0.95 %, the excess of the trend corrections is no longer detectable with this network. Assuming a centred error, their one-sided 90 % bound on the annual error is 2.6–2.7 %, compared with 2.2 % for one year on site. Measured against the true irradiance, only the two transfers based on the nearest stations remain worse than on-site adaptation across the whole network (permutation test with Holm correction). On the Tier 1 stations alone, no transfer is worse. A bias–latitude line with prediction intervals is provided for sites within the study domain. For direct normal irradiance (DNI), no transfer cost is established after correction for multiple comparisons. One year of measurement is not enough to pin down its bias.

title: A SMOTE enhanced multi stream deep learning ensemble for credit card fraud detection
abstract: Credit card fraud detection is highly imbalanced, making minority-class metrics and deployment efficiency more informative than accuracy alone. This study proposes SMOTE-EnsembleNet (SENet), combining CNN, BiLSTM, and Transformer streams through learnable cross-attention fusion. Among 100%, 200%, and 500% SMOTE ratios with focal loss, 200% SMOTE achieved the best overall balance. SENet obtained AUC-ROC values of 0.9967 (95% CI 0.9955–0.9979), 0.9567 (95% CI 0.9542–0.9592), and 0.9923 (95% CI 0.9911–0.9935) on ULB, IEEE-CIS, and PaySim, respectively. Compared with no SMOTE, AUC-ROC improved by 1.55, 1.55, and 1.34 percentage points, while cross-attention improved AUC-ROC by 0.22 percentage points over concatenation. Fold-level significance testing ((p < 0.05)) was conducted against all tuned baselines. SENet achieved 12.4 ms inference latency per transaction on an NVIDIA A100 GPU while supporting interpretable error and feature-importance analyses. AUC-ROC and AUC-PR are threshold-independent, whereas precision, recall, and F1-score are reported separately in the experiments. The 12.4 ms latency applies only to the stated NVIDIA A100 configuration. Cross-attention additionally improved AUC-PR by 1.3 percentage points over concatenation, and the small differences between 200% and 500% SMOTE are interpreted together with fold-level statistical tests.

title: New results on hypercube coloring problem from linear codes over Z2k
abstract: This paper is concerned with the hypercube coloring problem. Let 𝜒 ℓ ⁡ ( 𝑚 ) be the minimum number of colors needed to color the vertices of a hypercube with 2 𝑚 vertices such that every two vertices with Hamming distance ≤ ℓ have different colors. Using linear codes over ℤ 2 𝑘 (the ring of integers modulo 2 𝑘 ) and the generalized Gray map, we establish a connection between the parameters of linear codes over ℤ 2 𝑘 and 𝜒 ℓ ⁡ ( 𝑚 ) . Furthermore, we obtain some new upper bounds on 𝜒 ℓ ⁡ ( 𝑚 ) . In some cases, the new upper bounds are tighter than the previously best known results. In particular, we determine the exact values 𝜒 5 ⁡ ( 1 4 ) = 2 8 and 𝜒 4 ⁡ ( 1 3 ) = 2 7 .

title: Reflective Compositional Grounding for Natural-Language-to-SPARQL
abstract: Natural-language query generation over large knowledge graphs embodies the classical vocabulary problem in human-systems communication. Questions express concepts through wording and compositions that can differ substantially from the target schema, while limited model context requires selective access to schema information. We present an NL2SPARQL framework that places conceptual compositionality at the center of query interpretation and connects it to the relational composition required for binding and query construction. A fixed concept encoder represents compound expressions jointly, and schema candidates are ranked using semantic similarity, type compatibility, and hierarchy proximity. Reflective refinement critically examines how the grounded meanings are realized through argument bindings, joins, and operator scope. Diagnosed semantic discrepancies guide revisions to the responsible stage. We formalise a monotone refinement discipline that accumulates scoped interpretation requirements and establish conditions under which changes to the composed process preserve previously validated interpretations. Across five benchmark/knowledge-graph targets, mean schema recall@10 increases from 0.712 to 0.837. With retrieval held fixed, reflective prompt rewriting adds 2.27-3.33 answer-F1 points. These experiments evaluate the grounding and refinement mechanisms, while the formal analysis specifies the stronger requirements for conservative adaptation across queries.

title: Qudit Implementation of the Rodeo Algorithm - 1D Ising Model Dataset
abstract: Qudits, the multi-level generalization of qubits, provide a natural extension of the binary paradigm in quantum computation and offer new opportunities to enhance algorithmic performance. Beyond their direct applicability to the simulation of multi-level quantum systems, higher-dimensional ancillae can improve sampling efficiency in quantum algorithms by enabling the simultaneous implementation of multiple control operations, thereby reducing circuit complexity. In this work, we pursue three main objectives. First, we present a formulation of the Rodeo algorithm employing a general $d$-level ancilla qudit. Second, we introduce the concept of the \emph{Rodeo kernel}, defined as a two-frequency interferometer, which acts as a spectral filter in the energy domain. Finally, we propose a microcanonical protocol for the Rodeo algorithm. This protocol enables the estimation of entropic quantities through a single energy sweep and admits a natural interpretation as a Gaussian convolution of the density of states. To support the theoretical analysis, we perform numerical evaluations of the corresponding quantum circuit using ancilla qudits of dimensions three, four, and five. The simulations are performed for the one-dimensional Ising model, considering both spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ and spin-$1$ particles. The ancilla qutrit implementation exhibits an $18\%$ reduction in fluctuations compared to the qubit implementation. Our results show that the qudits provide a framework for spectral analysis and thermodynamic characterization of multi-level quantum systems.

title: Clause Linkage in Brazilian Portuguese Narratives: Evidence from Enhanced Dependency Annotation
abstract: This paper explores the potential of Enhanced and Extended Enhanced Universal Dependencies for narrative analysis in Brazilian Portuguese, focusing on how enhanced dependency relations contribute to clause linkage. The study examines narrative sentences annotated in CoNLL-U format and compares basic and enhanced dependency layers. The results show that enhanced dependencies are particularly useful for recovering implicit subject relations in Portuguese and for enriching clause relations through information from prepositions and conjunctions. These enhancements enable a more explicit representation of participant continuity and event relations in narratives, supporting the transition from syntactic dependency analysis to richer semantic annotation.

title: Vocabulary-constrained rewriting and translation for dictionary-based sign language avatars, code
abstract: Code of a study that measures how much a dictionary-based International Sign (IS) avatar with several hundred signs fingerspells in English meeting transcripts (AMI Meeting Corpus) and written sentences (FLORES-200), and whether rewording the text, or translating text from Greek, French, Spanish and German, into words that the avatar can sign avoids the fingerspelling without changing the meaning. The code replaces words without a sign by WordNet synonyms or by similar words judged by word vectors, rewrites and translates text with EuroLLM-1.7B-Instruct, with and without a llama.cpp grammar that restricts the output to words with a sign, translates with NLLB-200-distilled-600M, estimates the fingerspelling and signing time of a dictionary avatar, scores the meaning kept with COMET, chrF, sentence embeddings and mutual entailment, analyses the failures of restricted rewriting and writes the tables and figures of the article. Every model runs on an ordinary processor. The system outputs, scores and analyses are in the data deposit https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23396571.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Correction and Mutual Correction in Multi-Agent Systems: A Feedback-Driven Framework for Dynamic Error Repair
abstract: Multi-agent systems can improve the reliability of intelligent problem-solving through error detection, iterative refinement, and information exchange. However, two fundamental correction mechanisms present different advantages and limitations. Self-correction allows an agent to identify and repair errors within its own reasoning or behavior, whereas mutual correction enables agents to inspect, challenge, and improve one another's outputs. Continuous reliance on either mechanism may introduce undesirable behavior, including persistent individual reasoning errors, redundant refinement, uncritical acceptance of peer feedback, and unnecessary communication costs. This paper proposes Adaptive Self–Mutual Correction (ASMC), a feedback-driven framework that dynamically switches between self-correction and mutual correction according to observed correction outcomes, estimated residual errors, agent disagreement, confidence calibration, and computational costs. Rather than assuming that independent correction or collaborative correction is universally superior, ASMC treats the selection of a correction mechanism as a dynamic decision problem. The framework includes independent error diagnosis, peer-based verification, correction-quality estimation, adaptive mode selection, and outcome-based evaluation. A formal optimization objective is introduced to balance task accuracy, correction effectiveness, computational efficiency, and the preservation of valid solutions. The framework is designed to support heterogeneous or homogeneous intelligent agents, including software agents, robotic agents, planning systems, and language-model-based agents. A theoretical analysis identifies conditions under which adaptive selection can outperform fixed correction policies, while also clarifying the assumptions required for such guarantees. An experimental protocol is proposed to evaluate the framework against self-correction-only, mutual-correction-only, fixed alternating, and other adaptive baselines. evidence.title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Correction and Mutual Correction in Multi-Agent Systems: A Feedback-Driven Framework for Dynamic Error Repair
evidence.abstract: Multi-agent systems can improve the reliability of intelligent problem-solving through error detection, iterative refinement, and information exchange. However, two fundamental correction mechanisms present different advantages and limitations. Self-correction allows an agent to identify and repair errors within its own reasoning or behavior, whereas mutual correction enables agents to inspect, challenge, and improve one another's outputs. Continuous reliance on either mechanism may introduce undesirable behavior, including persistent individual reasoning errors, redundant refinement, uncritical acceptance of peer feedback, and unnecessary communication costs. This paper proposes Adaptive Self–Mutual Correction (ASMC), a feedback-driven framework that dynamically switches between self-correction and mutual correction according to observed correction outcomes, estimated residual errors, agent disagreement, confidence calibration, and computational costs. Rather than assuming that independent correction or collaborative correction is universally superior, ASMC treats the selection of a correction mechanism as a dynamic decision problem. The framework includes independent error diagnosis, peer-based verification, correction-quality estimation, adaptive mode selection, and outcome-based evaluation. A formal optimization objective is introduced to balance task accuracy, correction effectiveness, computational efficiency, and the preservation of valid solutions. The framework is designed to support heterogeneous or homogeneous intelligent agents, including software agents, robotic agents, planning systems, and language-model-based agents. A theoretical analysis identifies conditions under which adaptive selection can outperform fixed correction policies, while also clarifying the assumptions required for such guarantees. An experimental protocol is proposed to evaluate the framework against self-correction-only, mutual-correction-only, fixed alternating, and other adaptive baselines. The proposed approach provides a general research direction for dynamically coordinating individual error repair and collaborative error repair in multi-agent intelligence.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Reflection and Mutual Reflection in Multi-Agent Systems: A Unified Framework for Dynamic Reflective Intelligence
abstract: Multi-agent systems can improve problem-solving through iterative reflection, error detection, information exchange, and collaborative decision-making. However, existing reflective processes often rely on fixed interaction patterns, such as allowing each agent to revise its own output independently or requiring multiple agents to critique one another throughout a predefined sequence. These static patterns may be inefficient when independent reflection is sufficient, yet inadequate when an agent's reasoning is constrained by its own assumptions or incomplete information. This paper proposes Adaptive Switching between Self-Reflection and Mutual Reflection (ASSMR), a unified framework that dynamically selects between two complementary reflective mechanisms according to the evolving state of a multi-agent system. Self-reflection enables an agent to examine and revise its own reasoning, decisions, or actions without requiring external reflective input. Mutual reflection enables agents to evaluate, challenge, and refine one another's outputs through structured interactions. The proposed framework estimates the relative utility of these mechanisms using indicators such as uncertainty, unresolved errors, disagreement, information diversity, reflection progress, communication cost, and observed task performance. A switching controller then selects an appropriate reflective mode, determines the participating agents, and evaluates whether further reflection is beneficial. The framework also incorporates adaptive switching thresholds, bounded reflection cycles, historical feedback, and safeguards against premature consensus and repetitive reasoning. Unlike approaches that simply combine individual reasoning with multi-agent debate, ASSMR treats the selection and transition between reflective modes as an explicit system-level decision problem. This paper formalizes the framework, presents a reference algorithm, develops research propositions, and outlines an experimental protocol for evaluating effectiveness, efficiency, robustness, and reflective diversity across heterogeneous multi-agent environments. The framework is a methodological proposal; its comparative advantages and empirical performance remain to be established through experiments.

title: A Geospatial Operational Event Knowledge Graph for Traceable Air–Ground Robotic Inspection in Grain-Reserve Warehouses
abstract: Intelligent monitoring in grain-reserve warehouses increasingly combines fixed sensors, UAVs, quadruped robots, human review, and site information systems, yet the resulting operational records are typically stored separately. This fragmentation makes it difficult to reconstruct how a detected problem evolves from observation to execution, evidence, and review, and limits traceable data-driven decision support. To address this issue, this study proposes a Geospatial Operational Event Knowledge Graph (GOEKG) that uses a stable managed-event identity to organize geographic anchors, source provenance, air–ground tasks, evidence, review, and lifecycle states within a property graph. The framework combines source-record normalization and graph mapping with competency queries and operational-semantic constraints for temporal order, spatial continuity, review reachability, lifecycle transitions, and provenance-aware reconciliation. A Panqiao warehouse case is used to instantiate and evaluate the graph. The case instantiated 11 reference-case nodes and 15 typed relations; six competency queries recovered the corresponding paths with temporal and spatial continuity across both robot branches. Controlled mutations of a source-derived record fixture returned UNKNOWN for missing temporal anchors, resolved spatial conflicts by explicit rules, and rejected temporal-order, spatial-linkage, and unauthorized-closure violations. A Neo4j benchmark on synthetic fixtures scaled from 1000 to 50,000 events. Secondary evaluations measured chronological alert-type relation completion and strict temporal fixed-snapshot follow-up candidate ranking. Under the latter protocol, Context-only achieved Macro-F1 0.783 and balanced accuracy 0.836, while Full context achieved average precision 0.952 and prioritized Pending Verification records in the limited-budget queue. The fixed-snapshot analysis supports context-assisted review prioritization under a retrospective event-time protocol. GOEKG therefore provides a traceable event-centered integration layer for intelligent monitoring and review-oriented operational decision support.

title: Constrained dissipation and the lifetime of quantum many-body scars
abstract: We investigate the fate of quantum many-body scars in the PXP model subject to Markovian dissipation. We show that when local jump operators respect the same symmetries of the Hamiltonian the full Liouvillian spectrum displays a tower of states with properties analogous to standard quantum scars: large overlaps with Néel states and equally spaced gaps in the imaginary part of the eigenvalues, set by a single frequency. Whether the long-time dynamics is dominated by scars is determined by the real parts of the eigenvalues, which are set by the ratio between the two relaxation rates γ_{pm} describing spin flips down-to-up or up-to-down respectively. For asymmetric dissipation (γ_+ > γ_-) the scarred eigenvalues have the smallest real parts: the resulting enhanced fidelity oscillations are further stabilized by staggered jump operators. In contrast, replacing the full projection operator in the dissipators with a partial one breaks the symmetries of the problem and is seen to destroy dissipative scars altogether.

title: Self-Calibrated Subspace Robust PCA for Parameter-Free Removal of Mixed Noise and Line Stripes in Hyperspectral Images
abstract: Hyperspectral images (HSIs) are often corrupted by Gaussian noise, impulses and stripes whose intensities vary across bands. The representative coefficient correlated total variation (RCCTV) model restores HSIs efficiently, but it lacks Gaussian and stripe terms, and its noise-aware extensions require the noise level and a stripe budget to be specified in advance. This article proposes a self-calibrated RCCTV (SC-RCCTV) model, in which the noise parameters are estimated adaptively during the iterations. A band-wise dense term and line-constant column and row stripe terms are introduced into RCCTV. The noise level of each band is initialized by a stripe-invariant median absolute deviation estimator and refined online from the residual, which turns the separation of sparse and dense noise into a band-adaptive Huber loss, and the stripe thresholds follow from a significance test whose false-alarm rate can be predicted analytically. No parameter is tuned for a specific image, and every subproblem of the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) solver is solved in closed form. Under line stripes, SC-RCCTV outperforms the parameter-free FastHyMix by 8.17 dB on native-size cubes, and, without any noise information, it exceeds S3TTV, which is given the true noise parameters, by 1.52 dB while running more than 1,900 times faster. On average, it stays within 0.01 dB of the same model given the true noise levels, and its online calibration improves on a two-stage estimate-then-denoise scheme. Experiments on real Indian Pines and Urban data further delineate its scope for stripes that do not span entire lines.
